Autonomic Nervous System — Introduction

A foundational walkthrough of the ANS: how the sympathetic and parasympathetic divisions are organized anatomically, how their neurotransmitters are synthesized and released, how their receptors transduce a signal into a cellular effect, and how every one of those steps explains a real drug or a real bedside finding.

Exam Questions

🎯Learning Objectives

By the end of this topic, you should be able to:

  • Differentiate the anatomical origin (thoracolumbar vs craniosacral) and fiber length pattern of the sympathetic and parasympathetic divisions.
  • Explain why the adrenal medulla is a modified sympathetic ganglion and how that explains its unique innervation and secretion.
  • Trace the synthesis pathway of norepinephrine and epinephrine from tyrosine, and name each enzyme.
  • Classify all major ANS receptors (nicotinic, muscarinic, alpha, beta) by their G-protein coupling and downstream second messenger.
  • Predict the physiological effect of sympathetic vs parasympathetic stimulation on every major organ system.
  • Connect each receptor mechanism to a real drug used in clinical practice (asthma, BPH, glaucoma, anaphylaxis, pre-anesthesia).

Course Roadmap

This lecture is an introductory pass through the ANS — broad strokes now, clinical/pharmacological depth returns later in the curriculum.

Anatomy → Neurotransmitters → Receptors → Organ Effects → Pharmacology → Clinical →

🧭Where the ANS Fits

The nervous system's functions divide into two broad categories:

Autonomic (Involuntary) Governs the majority of body functions: secretion, digestion, absorption, circulation (heart and blood vessels), respiration, sweating. Entirely involuntary.
Somatic (Voluntary) Controls voluntary skeletal muscle activity and somatic sensation — the focus of upcoming lectures in this course.

💡Key Concepts at a Glance

Anatomy

Sympathetic = thoracolumbar (T1–L2/3). Parasympathetic = craniosacral (CN 3,7,9,10 + S2–S4).

Physiology

Parasympathetic = rest and digest, anabolic. Sympathetic = fight or flight, catabolic.

Pharmacology

Receptor G-protein coupling (Gq / Gi / Gs) determines the second messenger and, ultimately, the drug target.

⭐⭐⭐ Why This Matters Every autonomic drug class you'll ever prescribe — beta-agonists, alpha-blockers, anticholinergics, parasympathomimetics — works by exploiting exactly the receptor logic taught in this lecture. Understanding the mechanism here means you never have to memorize a drug effect again; you can derive it.
Neuroanatomy

Division of the Autonomic Nervous System

Sympathetic vs Parasympathetic — origin, fiber architecture, and the special case of the adrenal medulla.

Figure. Overview of nervous system division — central vs peripheral, and the autonomic split into sympathetic and parasympathetic outflow.

🔀Sympathetic vs Parasympathetic: Origins

Sympathetic

"Sympas" — the emotional system

The name comes from sympathy — linked to emotion, excitement, anger, and joy. Most sympathetic functions track with emotional and physical arousal: heart rate rises when upset, blood pressure climbs, sweating appears under stress, appetite may increase.

Anatomical origin Thoracolumbar — fibers emerge from the entire thoracic spinal cord (T1–T12) and the upper lumbar segments (L1, L2, and often L3).
Parasympathetic

"Para" — running alongside

"Para" means parallel — in the sense of adjacent and accompanying. A parasympathetic fiber travels alongside its sympathetic counterpart to the same organ (e.g., both reach the heart), hence "para-sympathetic" = the one running next to the sympathetic.

Anatomical origin Craniosacral — 5 cranial nerves (III, V, VII, IX, X) plus the 5 sacral nerves (S1–S5, functionally S2–S4).

The Cranial Contributors to Parasympathetic Outflow

Cranial NerveNumberStructure Supplied
OculomotorCN IIISphincter pupillae, ciliary muscle
TrigeminalCN V(Pathway carrier for parasympathetic fibers to glands)
FacialCN VIILacrimal, submandibular, sublingual glands
GlossopharyngealCN IXParotid gland
VagusCN XHeart, lungs, most of the GI tract

🔗Preganglionic vs Postganglionic Fibers

All efferent (motor/response) autonomic pathways are two-neuron chains: a preganglionic fiber synapses in an autonomic ganglion onto a postganglionic fiber, which then reaches the target organ. This mirrors the presynaptic/postsynaptic relationship you've already learned — the key difference is that here, the synapse (the ganglion) sits out in the peripheral nervous system.

Parasympathetic fiber lengths Long preganglionic, short postganglionic. The ganglion often sits right at, or even inside, the target organ — so the postganglionic fiber can be extremely short, sometimes located in, on, or near the organ itself.
Sympathetic fiber lengths Short preganglionic, long postganglionic. Ganglia sit close to the spinal cord (paravertebral chain), then long postganglionic fibers fan out to distant organs — producing a more diffuse, widespread effect.

⭐Special Case: The Adrenal Medulla

⭐⭐⭐ Must Know The adrenal medulla receives only a preganglionic sympathetic fiber — it has no postganglionic fiber at all. That's because the adrenal medulla is itself a modified autonomic ganglion. During development it lost its postganglionic fiber and, instead of passing the signal to a neuron, it releases hormones (catecholamines) directly into the circulation — making it functionally an endocrine gland.

Because of this modification, the adrenal medulla secretes the catecholamines directly into the bloodstream:

Adrenaline (Epinephrine) Noradrenaline (Norepinephrine) Dopamine
Source: ANS Introduction lecture, Batch 44 — curated by Dr. Hassan Salaheldeen.
Neurophysiology

Neurotransmitters of the ANS

What a chemical messenger is, which transmitter is released where, and exactly how norepinephrine and epinephrine are synthesized step-by-step.

💬What Is a Chemical Messenger?

Definition: A chemical messenger is a chemical substance secreted by one cell to conduct a message to another cell. When that message is a nerve impulse, the messenger is specifically called a neurotransmitter.

Neurotransmitters are released either:

  • At the ending of a preganglionic fiber, to transmit the impulse to the postganglionic neuron, or
  • At the ending of a postganglionic fiber, to transmit the impulse to the target organ.

🧪The Main Transmitters

Main

Acetylcholine

The principal neurotransmitter of the ANS — released by all preganglionic fibers of both divisions.

Sympathetic

Norepinephrine

Also called noradrenaline. Released by most sympathetic postganglionic fibers.

Adrenal

Epinephrine

Also called adrenaline. Released mainly by the adrenal medulla into the circulation.

Where do the names come from? Epinephrine and norepinephrine both derive from the adrenal gland (also called the suprarenal gland). The kidney's functional unit is the nephron — so "supra-renal" became "epi-nephr-ine": the substance from "above the nephron."

Co-transmitters

Several molecules act as accessory co-transmitters released alongside the primary transmitter:

VIP (Vasoactive Intestinal Peptide) Neuropeptide Y Nitric Oxide

Example: VIP co-released with acetylcholine increases blood supply to the salivary glands and is also found in genital/reproductive tissue.

⚙️Acetylcholine — Synthesis & Distribution

Synthesis

Acetylcholine is synthesized from choline (a nitrogenous base) plus activated acetate, catalyzed by the enzyme choline acetyltransferase.

⭐⭐⭐ Nicotinic Receptors Acetylcholine released by every preganglionic fiber (sympathetic and parasympathetic alike) binds nicotinic receptors on the postganglionic neuron. Named because they are excited by a moderate dose of nicotine and inhibited by a large dose — the classic pharmacology finding that gave them their name.

Three Exceptions Where Postganglionic Fibers Release ACh Instead of NE

Even though most sympathetic postganglionic fibers release norepinephrine, three important exceptions release acetylcholine:

TargetFiber TypeFunctional Name
Thermoregulatory sweat glands (most of the body)CholinergicWidespread heat-regulating sweating
Localized sweat glands (palms & soles)Adrenergic (NE)Stress-induced sweating
Blood vessels of skeletal muscleCholinergicVasodilation to support exercise
High Yield Sweat glands are functionally split in two: the thermoregulatory glands (whole body, heat-driven, cholinergic) vs the stress-induced glands (palms and soles, emotion-driven, adrenergic). This is a classic exam distinction.
Figure. Dual innervation pattern of sweat glands — cholinergic thermoregulatory fibers vs adrenergic stress-induced fibers to palms and soles.

🧬Norepinephrine & Epinephrine — Full Synthesis Pathway

Figure. Complete biosynthetic pathway: Tyrosine → DOPA → Dopamine → Norepinephrine → Epinephrine, with each converting enzyme labeled.

Norepinephrine is synthesized from the amino acid tyrosine in a stepwise pathway:

  1. Tyrosine is itself essentially monohydroxyphenylalanine — phenylalanine with one hydroxyl group added.
  2. Tyrosine hydroxylase adds a second hydroxyl group → DOPA (dihydroxyphenylalanine).
  3. DOPA decarboxylase removes the carboxyl group → Dopamine.
  4. Dopamine β-hydroxylase hydroxylates dopamine → Norepinephrine. This is the final product for sympathetic postganglionic fibers.
  5. In the adrenal medulla (and brain only), the enzyme phenylethanolamine N-methyltransferase (PNMT) adds a methyl group to norepinephrine → Epinephrine.
⭐⭐⭐ Must Know — Where Epinephrine Is Made The methylation step that converts NE → Epinephrine occurs only in the adrenal medulla and the brain — not in ordinary sympathetic postganglionic fibers. This is why sympathetic nerve endings release norepinephrine, while the adrenal medulla releases a mix of both.

Bonus: Decarboxylation Pattern Across Amino Acids

Pattern recognition trick Removing the carboxyl group from an amino acid is a recurring biochemical theme: Histidine → Histamine; 5-hydroxytryptophan → Serotonin (5-hydroxytryptamine); DOPA → Dopamine. Recognizing "decarboxylation = amine" saves memorization time across biochemistry and pharmacology.

🎯Why the Methyl Group Matters — Receptor Affinity

Clinical logic Adding a methyl group to norepinephrine (making epinephrine) changes its receptor affinity:
  • Norepinephrine (no methyl group): higher affinity for alpha receptors than beta.
  • Epinephrine (methylated): higher affinity for beta receptors than alpha.
This is why sympathetic activity is classically associated with alpha-mediated vasoconstriction (especially alpha-1) — most sympathetic postganglionic endings release norepinephrine, which favors alpha receptors.
Source: ANS Introduction lecture, Batch 44 — curated by Dr. Hassan Salaheldeen.
Neurophysiology

Receptors & Signal Transduction

Every ANS receptor, its G-protein family, its second messenger, and the one rule that predicts smooth muscle behavior everywhere in the body.

🔑Nicotinic Receptors — Ligand-Gated Ion Channels

Nicotinic receptors are unusual: they are both a receptor and an ion channel at once — ligand-gated channels for sodium and potassium, though predominantly permeable to sodium influx. Found at every ganglionic synapse (preganglionic → postganglionic) in both divisions.

📡Gq-Coupled Receptors — M1, M3, M5, Alpha-1

Figure. G-protein coupled receptor signaling cascades — Gq → phospholipase C → IP3/DAG; Gi → ↓cAMP; Gs → ↑cAMP → PKA.

M1, M3, M5 (muscarinic) and alpha-1 (adrenergic) receptors couple to Gq (stimulatory in this context) and activate the enzyme phospholipase C. This cleaves membrane phosphatidylinositol diphosphate into two second messengers:

IP3 (Inositol triphosphate) Triggers release of calcium from the endoplasmic/sarcoplasmic reticulum into the cytoplasm.
DAG (Diacylglycerol) Activates protein kinase C, which opens calcium channels, driving calcium influx from the extracellular space.
⭐⭐⭐ The Master Rule Both pathways converge on one outcome: increased intracellular calcium. And the rule that makes this whole receptor system predictable: whenever calcium rises in smooth muscle, contraction results. This single rule explains alpha-1 vasoconstriction and M3 bronchoconstriction in one stroke.

🔻Gi-Coupled Receptors — M2, M4, Alpha-2

M2, M4 (muscarinic) and alpha-2 (adrenergic) receptors couple to Gi, which inhibits adenylate cyclase — lowering intracellular cyclic AMP.

Worked example: Acetylcholine in the heart Acetylcholine acting on M2 receptors in the heart decreases cyclic AMP, producing four negative effects: negative chronotropic (↓rate), negative inotropic (↓contractility), negative dromotropic (↓conduction velocity), and negative bathmotropic (↓excitability).

M2 receptors have a second mechanism beyond lowering cAMP: they directly open potassium channels. Potassium efflux causes hyperpolarization of pacemaker cells, slowing the rate of spontaneous depolarization (the pacemaker potential) — a second, independent way acetylcholine reduces heart rate.

🔺Gs-Coupled Receptors — Beta-1, Beta-2, Beta-3

All three beta receptor subtypes couple to Gs, which stimulates adenylate cyclase, raising cyclic AMP. Cyclic AMP activates protein kinase A — a transferase enzyme that phosphorylates target proteins (channels, pumps, enzymes) to activate them (analogous to hexokinase phosphorylating glucose in glycolysis).

In the heart specifically Protein kinase A phosphorylates calcium channels (opening them) and potassium channels (closing them) simultaneously. More calcium in, less potassium out = faster depolarization, increased rate, and increased contractility. This is the mechanistic basis of sympathetic/adrenaline cardiac stimulation.

📋Complete Receptor Reference Table

ReceptorG-Protein2nd Messenger EffectExample Location / Action

M2, M4 & Alpha-2Gi↓cAMP, ↑K⁺ effluxM2: ↓heart rate

Organ Systems

Organ-by-Organ Autonomic Effects

Every organ system, its sympathetic response, its parasympathetic response, and the receptor driving each — the master reference table for this lecture.

⭐⭐⭐ Big Picture First Parasympathetic activity dominates at rest — "rest and digest," mostly anabolic (energy storage). Sympathetic activity dominates during exercise, emotion, and stress — "fight or flight," mostly catabolic (energy mobilization: glycogenolysis, lipolysis). This is sometimes remembered as the system of 3 F's: stimulated by Fright, to Fight or Flight.
Figure. Full-body comparison of parasympathetic ("rest and digest") vs sympathetic ("fight or flight") effects, organized by outflow level (cranial, thoracic, lumbar, sacral).

❤️Cardiovascular System

OrganSympatheticParasympathetic
Heart rate & contractility↑ via β1↓ (mainly atria — ventricular parasympathetic innervation is very sparse)
Arterioles (skin, GIT, renal)Constriction—
Arterioles (skeletal muscle)Dilation (M, β2) or Constriction (α1)—
Systemic veinsDilation (β2) or Constriction (α)—
Endothelium (arteriole)—Releases EDRF (nitric oxide)
Why is the intrinsic SA node rate ~105 bpm, but resting HR ~75? Without any autonomic input at all, the SA node's intrinsic firing rate is about 105 bpm. Continuous parasympathetic (vagal) tone brings it down to the resting ~75 bpm. This is why the normal resting range spans 60–100 bpm — it reflects the balance of ongoing sympathetic and parasympathetic tone on the SA node.
Naming logic of the medullary cardiovascular centers The vasomotor center is named for its dominant effect on blood vessels (sympathetic-driven), while the cardioinhibitory center is named for its dominant effect on the heart (parasympathetic/vagal-driven) — reflecting which division dominates which structure.

🫁Deep Dive: Asthma Pharmacology

Figure. The two classic inhaler colors used worldwide: the blue-and-white reliever (β2 agonist, e.g., salbutamol) and the orange-and-white preventer (inhaled steroid).

Why combine a β2 agonist with a steroid?

Steroids potentiate catecholamine action through two mechanisms:

  1. Steroids act via intracellular receptors that stimulate specific gene transcription — one product is the β-receptor itself, so steroids increase the number of β2 receptors available.
  2. Steroids induce the enzyme phenylethanolamine N-methyltransferase (PNMT), the enzyme that converts norepinephrine to epinephrine — increasing the supply of the more β-selective catecholamine.
⭐⭐⭐ Status Asthmaticus In status asthmaticus — a severe asthma attack unresponsive to beta agonists, steroids, leukotriene antagonists, aminophylline/theophylline, and anticholinergics — epinephrine is used as a rescue drug. It is the most potent bronchodilator known, and even though its non-selective β1 activity causes tachycardia and palpitations, that trade-off is accepted because nothing else works in this emergency.

🩺Deep Dive: Atropine's Two Clinical Uses

Dentistry

Excess parasympathetic-driven watery salivation forces continuous swallowing, making it hard for a dentist to work with the mouth open. Atropine dries the mouth, allowing uninterrupted treatment.

Pre-Anesthesia

Given before general anesthesia to dry respiratory tract secretions. An endotracheal tube can irritate the airway; irritation increases secretions, and excess secretion risks blocking the tube — atropine reduces this risk.

Source: ANS Introduction lecture, Batch 44 — curated by Dr. Hassan Salaheldeen.
Clinical Correlations

Bringing the Basic Science to the Bedside

Where every receptor concept in this lecture shows up in real patients and real emergencies.

🚨 Status Asthmaticus ▾

A severe, life-threatening asthma attack that fails to respond to standard bronchodilator therapy — β2 agonists, steroids, leukotriene antagonists, methylxanthines (aminophylline/theophylline), and anticholinergics all fail. Epinephrine is given as a rescue agent because it remains the most potent bronchodilator known, working through both β1 and β2 receptors, despite the cardiac side effects (tachycardia, palpitations) that come from its non-selective β1 activity.

🫀 Anaphylactic & Septic Shock ▾

Both anaphylactic and septic shock involve massive, systemic vasodilation driven by excess nitric oxide production, causing profound hypotension. Epinephrine is the treatment of choice for anaphylaxis specifically — it counteracts the shock state through potent α1-mediated vasoconstriction (raising blood pressure) combined with β2-mediated bronchodilation (relieving airway compromise from bronchospasm/angioedema).

🚻 Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia (BPH) & Urinary Retention ▾

In BPH, prostate enlargement compresses the urethra and the internal sphincter mechanism, making urination difficult and causing urinary retention. Since the internal urethral sphincter contracts via α1 receptors, an α1-blocker (e.g., prazosin) relaxes the sphincter and facilitates urine flow.

👁️ Glaucoma ▾

Glaucoma involves elevated intraocular pressure from impaired aqueous humor drainage. Parasympathomimetic eye drops (e.g., pilocarpine) contract the ciliary muscle, which mechanically opens the canal of Schlemm, increasing aqueous humor drainage and lowering intraocular pressure.

🦷 Pre-Procedural Secretion Control ▾

Atropine (an anticholinergic/muscarinic antagonist) is used both in dentistry (to stop profuse watery salivation that forces continuous swallowing) and as a pre-anesthetic medication (to dry respiratory secretions before intubation, reducing the risk of the endotracheal tube being obstructed by secretions triggered by airway irritation).

🫁 Asthma Maintenance vs Rescue Therapy ▾

Standard asthma management pairs a β2 agonist (bronchodilation) with an inhaled steroid (potentiates the β2 agonist by upregulating receptor number and inducing PNMT). This combination is why the two-inhaler regimen (blue reliever + orange preventer) is the global standard, rather than relying on the β2 agonist alone.

Source: ANS Introduction lecture, Batch 44 — curated by Dr. Hassan Salaheldeen.
Memory Aids

Mnemonics & Memory Tricks

Quick recall devices distilled directly from the lecture's own explanations.

Anatomy

Sympathetic Origin

"Thoracolumbar" — T1 to L2/3. Think: sympathetic sits in the "middle" of the spinal cord (thoracic + upper lumbar), between the cranial and sacral origins of its parasympathetic counterpart.

Anatomy

Parasympathetic Origin

"Craniosacral" — the two "ends": cranial nerves (III, VII, IX, X) at the top, sacral nerves (S2–S4) at the bottom. Remember cranial nerves 3-7-9-10 by counting: 3, then odd numbers 7, 9, then 10.

Physiology

3 F's of Sympathetic Activation

Stimulated by Fright, leading to Fight or Flight. All three F's converge on one goal: mobilizing energy for muscle contraction.

Physiology

Rest & Digest vs Fight & Flight

Parasympathetic = anabolic, energy storage, dominant at rest. Sympathetic = catabolic, energy mobilization, dominant under stress/exercise. Storage vs spending.

Pharmacology

Nicotinic Receptor Naming

Excited by a moderate dose of nicotine, inhibited by a large dose. Same drug, opposite effect depending on dose — a classic pharmacology teaching point worth remembering verbatim.

Biochemistry

Decarboxylation → Amine Pattern

Histidine → Histamine. Tryptophan (via 5-HTP) → Serotonin. DOPA → Dopamine. Removing a carboxyl group from an amino acid tends to produce its "-amine" partner.

🧠The Master Calcium Rule

⭐⭐⭐ One Rule, Many Answers Whenever intracellular calcium rises in smooth muscle → contraction results. Apply this single rule to derive (not memorize) multiple receptor effects:
  • α1 (Gq → ↑Ca²⁺) → vasoconstriction, mydriasis, sphincter contraction
  • M3 (Gq → ↑Ca²⁺) → bronchoconstriction, gut sphincter relaxation exceptions aside, glandular secretion

🔠G-Protein Quick Table

G-proteinReceptorsEffectMemory Cue
GqM1, M3, M5, α1↑IP3/DAG → ↑Ca²⁺ → contraction"Q for Quake" — muscle shakes/contracts
GiM2, M4, α2↓cAMP → inhibition"I for Inhibit"
Gsβ1, β2, β3↑cAMP → stimulation"S for Stimulate"

Exam Preparation

High-Yield Exam Zone

Single-best-answer questions covering every high-yield point from the lecture. Tap an option to check your answer.

1. ⭐⭐⭐ Which organ receives ONLY a preganglionic sympathetic fiber, with no postganglionic fiber?
A. Heart
B. Adrenal medulla
C. Salivary gland
D. Bladder
The adrenal medulla is a modified autonomic ganglion that lost its postganglionic fiber and instead secretes catecholamines directly into the circulation, functioning as an endocrine gland.
2. ⭐⭐ The parasympathetic nervous system is described anatomically as:
A. Thoracolumbar
B. Cervicothoracic
C. Craniosacral
D. Lumbosacral
Parasympathetic outflow arises from four cranial nerves (III, VII, IX, X) and the sacral spinal segments (S2–S4) — hence "craniosacral."
3. ⭐⭐⭐ A drug that is a moderate-dose agonist but a high-dose antagonist at its own receptor best describes which receptor's classic pharmacology?
A. Nicotinic receptor
B. Muscarinic receptor
C. Beta-1 receptor
D. Alpha-2 receptor
Nicotinic receptors are excited by a moderate dose of nicotine and inhibited by a large dose — the origin of their name.
4. ⭐⭐⭐ Gq-coupled receptor activation in smooth muscle ultimately produces which effect?
A. Relaxation via ↓calcium
B. Contraction via ↑calcium
C. Relaxation via ↑cAMP
D. No effect
Gq → phospholipase C → IP3/DAG → increased intracellular calcium → contraction in smooth muscle, by the master rule taught in this lecture.
5. ⭐⭐ Which enzyme converts norepinephrine to epinephrine, and where does this occur?
A. Tyrosine hydroxylase; sympathetic nerve terminals
B. DOPA decarboxylase; adrenal cortex
C. Phenylethanolamine N-methyltransferase; adrenal medulla and brain
D. Dopamine β-hydroxylase; liver
PNMT methylates norepinephrine into epinephrine, and this step occurs only in the adrenal medulla and brain — not in ordinary sympathetic postganglionic fibers.
6. ⭐⭐ A patient in status asthmaticus, unresponsive to beta agonists and steroids, should receive:
A. Atropine
B. Prazosin
C. Pilocarpine
D. Epinephrine
Epinephrine is the most potent bronchodilator known, and it is used as a rescue agent in status asthmaticus despite causing tachycardia via β1 activity.
7. ⭐⭐ Which fibers innervate the thermoregulatory (whole-body) sweat glands?
A. Sympathetic cholinergic fibers
B. Sympathetic adrenergic fibers
C. Parasympathetic cholinergic fibers
D. Parasympathetic adrenergic fibers
Thermoregulatory sweat glands are sympathetically innervated but release acetylcholine (cholinergic) — one of the classic exceptions to the "sympathetic = norepinephrine" rule.
8. ⭐⭐⭐ A BPH patient with urinary retention benefits most from which drug class?
A. Beta-2 agonist
B. Alpha-1 blocker
C. Muscarinic agonist
D. Nicotinic antagonist
Alpha-1 blockers (e.g., prazosin) relax the internal urethral sphincter (which contracts via α1), facilitating urination in BPH-related retention.
9. ⭐ Norepinephrine, lacking a methyl group, has a higher affinity for which receptor type compared to epinephrine?
A. Beta receptors
B. Nicotinic receptors
C. Alpha receptors
D. Muscarinic receptors
Norepinephrine has higher affinity for alpha receptors than beta; the added methyl group on epinephrine shifts affinity toward beta receptors.
10. ⭐⭐ Pilocarpine treats glaucoma by:
A. Blocking beta-2 receptors in the eye
B. Relaxing the ciliary muscle
C. Increasing aqueous humor production
D. Contracting the ciliary muscle to open the canal of Schlemm
Pilocarpine, a parasympathomimetic, contracts the ciliary muscle, mechanically opening the canal of Schlemm and increasing aqueous humor drainage.
11. ⭐⭐ M2 muscarinic receptors decrease heart rate through two independent mechanisms: Gi-mediated ↓cAMP, and:
A. Opening calcium channels
B. Opening potassium channels causing hyperpolarization
C. Closing sodium channels
D. Activating phospholipase C
M2 receptors directly open potassium channels, causing potassium efflux and hyperpolarization of pacemaker cells, reducing the rate of spontaneous depolarization.
12. ⭐ Which best explains why inhaled corticosteroids potentiate beta-2 agonists in asthma therapy?
A. They increase beta receptor synthesis and induce PNMT
B. They directly open potassium channels
C. They block muscarinic receptors
D. They inhibit phospholipase C
Steroids act via intracellular receptors to increase transcription of specific genes, including the beta receptor itself and PNMT, amplifying catecholamine effect.

❓Rapid-Fire Viva Questions

Why is the adrenal medulla called a "modified ganglion"? ▾

Because embryologically and functionally it is a sympathetic ganglion that lost its postganglionic fiber and instead secretes its transmitters (as hormones) directly into the blood, making it an endocrine gland.

Why does the sympathetic system tend to have diffuse, widespread effects? ▾

Because its preganglionic fibers are short (synapsing near the spinal cord) while its postganglionic fibers are long, fanning out broadly to reach many distant organs from a compact origin.

Why does acetylcholine slow the heart rate? ▾

Via M2 receptors: (1) Gi-coupling lowers cyclic AMP, reducing pacemaker activity, and (2) direct opening of potassium channels hyperpolarizes pacemaker cells, both slowing the rate of spontaneous depolarization.

Why is epinephrine not used as first-line asthma therapy despite being the most potent bronchodilator? ▾

Because it is non-selective, also stimulating β1 receptors in the heart, causing tachycardia and palpitations — unwanted cardiac side effects that a selective β2 agonist avoids.

Last-Minute Review

Rapid Revision & Mind Map

One page. Everything you need the night before the exam.

📄One-Page Summary

Anatomy

Sympathetic = thoracolumbar (T1–L2/3), short preganglionic + long postganglionic, diffuse effect. Parasympathetic = craniosacral (CN III,VII,IX,X + S2–S4), long preganglionic + short postganglionic, localized effect. Adrenal medulla = modified ganglion, no postganglionic fiber, secretes catecholamines as endocrine gland.

Neurotransmitters

ACh: all preganglionic fibers, postganglionic parasympathetic, sweat glands (thermoregulatory) + skeletal muscle vessels. NE: most postganglionic sympathetic. Epi: adrenal medulla + brain only (via PNMT). Synthesis: Tyrosine → DOPA → Dopamine → NE → Epi.

Receptors

Nicotinic: ligand-gated Na⁺/K⁺ channel, all ganglia. Gq (M1,M3,M5,α1): ↑IP3/DAG/Ca²⁺ → contraction. Gi (M2,M4,α2): ↓cAMP + ↑K⁺ efflux → inhibition. Gs (β1,β2,β3): ↑cAMP → PKA → stimulation.

Clinical Drugs

Salbutamol (β2 agonist) + steroid: asthma. Epinephrine: status asthmaticus, anaphylaxis. Atropine: pre-anesthesia, dental drying. Prazosin (α1 blocker): BPH retention. Pilocarpine: glaucoma.

Reference

Difficult Medical Vocabulary

Key terms from this lecture, defined plainly.

Preganglionic fiber

The first neuron in an autonomic pathway, running from the CNS to a peripheral ganglion.

Postganglionic fiber

The second neuron in an autonomic pathway, running from the ganglion to the target organ.

Ganglion

A cluster of neuron cell bodies located outside the CNS, where preganglionic and postganglionic neurons synapse.

Thoracolumbar

Describes the sympathetic outflow, arising from thoracic and upper lumbar spinal segments.

Craniosacral

Describes the parasympathetic outflow, arising from cranial nerves and sacral spinal segments.

Catecholamines

A family of chemical messengers including dopamine, norepinephrine, and epinephrine, all derived from tyrosine.

Chronotropic

Affecting heart rate. "Negative chronotropic" = decreases heart rate.

Inotropic

Affecting the force of cardiac muscle contraction.

Dromotropic

Affecting the conduction velocity of the heart's electrical impulses.

Bathmotropic

Affecting the excitability of cardiac tissue.

Mydriasis

Pupil dilation, caused by sympathetic contraction of the radial muscle.

Miosis

Pupil constriction, caused by parasympathetic contraction of the circular muscle.

Lipolysis

Breakdown of stored fat into free fatty acids, stimulated by sympathetic activity.

Glycogenolysis

Breakdown of glycogen into glucose, stimulated by sympathetic activity.

Anabolic

Energy-storing metabolic state; associated with parasympathetic dominance.

Catabolic

Energy-mobilizing metabolic state; associated with sympathetic dominance.

Detrusor muscle

The smooth muscle layer of the urinary bladder wall.

Status asthmaticus

A severe, life-threatening asthma attack unresponsive to standard bronchodilator therapy.

Canal of Schlemm

The drainage channel for aqueous humor in the eye; its opening lowers intraocular pressure.

EDRF (Endothelium-Derived Relaxing Factor)

Nitric oxide released by endothelial cells that relaxes vascular smooth muscle.
